turn_text: My guest at this time is Kentucky Republican Senator Rand Paul. He joins me to discuss a number of key issues as the Senate plans to wrap up its work for the year this week. And Senator, always good to have you with us. Thank you.
Yeah. Thanks for having me, Greg. Well,

let's start with the spending bill that passed the House on Tuesday. It comes to the Senate later this week, $1.4 trillion split up into two different bills, both passed by a wide margin. So plenty of Republicans in favor, probably because there's increased military spending and a repeal of the Cadillac tax, amongst some other things. But it pretty much raises spending across the board. So what do you make of all this?

You know, I would say the nicest thing I can say about them is they would be an abomination. You know, they're terrible. I mean, it's just people who vote for this are not physically conservative. There's nothing conservative about this. This is blown through the caps. You know, when the Tea Party elected a bunch of people in 2010, that's when I came up here 2011. We were hot to go. We were, you know, putting caps on spending. We were opposing debt limits. we actually did get some caps in place all of those caps went away under republican leadership of the house senate and the presidency so it is a disappointment and so when i put forward something trying to free spending to balance the budget we'll get no democrats and less than half of the republicans in the senate and people just need to know that the republicans that are coming home to you and saying they're conservative and they want to balance the budget or not being honest with you and frankly We've got to do a better job in the Republican primaries of actually finding conservative legislators and sending some of these big government Republicans home.

turn_text: Not a lot of time left in our conversation, but two topics I want to get into that in that remaining time. I'm sure you're well aware of the Washington Post story, a devastating report last week claiming that the Bush and Obama administrations really had no idea what they were doing in Afghanistan and actively engaged in deceiving the American public. You're obviously well known for removing the U.S. from foreign military entanglements, but of course there's also an understandable concern that if there's not a U.S. presence there, Afghanistan quickly spirals into the breeding ground it was before 9-11. So what's your reaction to the report and what's the best policy going forward?

You know, it's an insult to our young men and women who volunteer for our armed services. They're brave. You know, they'll go where they're told. They will fight the fight that they're instructed to fight, but it's not fair to them if there isn't a mission. And there hasn't been a mission for at least a decade or more. The original mission was to go after those who attacked us on 9-11. I agreed with that mission. I would have voted for it. But in voting in 2011 to go after those who attacked us, in the first six months to a year, most of those people were killed or captured. You know, finally bin Laden was captured, but essentially there is no al Qaeda in Afghanistan. So people who say, oh, we've got to fight them over there. We'll fight them over here. That sort of logic that we have to occupy territory is sort of a last century kind of objective or last century kind of thought process. The thing is that there's so many places for terrorists to go. Why do they have to all be in Afghanistan? In fact, a lot of them are in Libya, a lot of them are in Syria, a lot of them are in Iraq, a lot of them are in Iran. There's a lot of different places for them to go. We can't occupy all those places. The other thing about Afghanistan is not only is it a mess, it's an extraordinarily expensive mess. You know, it's costing us $50 billion a year, so it's bleeding us dry. And people who say, if you leave, there'll be chaos. We're there and it's chaos. The Taliban has been gradually taking more and more countryside with us there. So frankly, I think the Afghanis who live there need to step up. People of Islam who believe in a moderate, you know, reasonable, rational, peaceful Islam need to stand up to the radicals and they need to fight them. We can't always be doing the fighting for everyone. It's extraordinarily expensive, but people cannot win their liberty if somebody else wins it for them. They've got to stand up and fight.
